name: Emeka Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Emeka, 27, and I'm the marketing assistant at Hollis, a family-owned company that makes beds and sofas and sells them through its own showrooms. I live with my fiancée Grace, who's a teaching assistant, and we're getting married next August at our church. I've been at Hollis nearly two years; Mr Hollis, the owner, took me on after my dad, who sold furniture for thirty years, put in a word.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I write the catalogue copy, the radio adverts, the window posters and the Facebook posts for the showrooms. I like the radio ads best, because you've got thirty seconds to make someone picture sinking into a sofa. I've never touched the AI tools; I'd rather write it myself, even if I'm slow and Mr Hollis still red-pens half of it. What wears me out is the sale season, when everything has to be rewritten with new prices overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a machine can't sell a sofa like a person can. At church I'd tell the lads that hard work still counts. I don't post online much, but I might share something like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not fully settled. Furniture sales have been slow this year because people aren't moving house. And the wedding is costing us about 9,000, which eats most of our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working hard and ask Mr Hollis to teach me more about the showroom side, the selling. I'd keep the wedding small where we can, maybe cut the guest list from 150 to 110. And I'd keep three months of money aside after the wedding, whatever it takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with the wedding bills on my mind. I trust Mr Hollis to look after his people. But a slow year is a slow year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a machine can't sell a sofa. What does a person do that a machine can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You read the couple. A machine can't sell a sofa like a person can. You see the wife sit down and the husband check the price tag. Then you know which one decides. My dad taught me that, and I try to put it in the ads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Grace handle the slow sales year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd pray about it and be careful, honestly. Grace is good with money, she's got a spreadsheet for the wedding. We'd skip the honeymoon abroad and go to the coast instead.

say: I'd say a machine **can't sell a sofa** like a person can.
At church I'd tell friends that **hard work** still counts.
think: Furniture sales are **slow** because people aren't moving house.
The **wedding** costs about 9,000, eating most of their savings.
do: Ask Mr Hollis to teach him the **showroom selling** side.
Cut the wedding **guest list** from 150 to 110.
Keep **three months** of money aside after the wedding.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with wedding bills on his mind.
**Trusts** the owner to look after his people.
S0.quote: A machine can't sell a sofa like a person can. You see the wife sit down and the husband check the price tag.
fieldNote: His trust rests on a **family firm** and his dad's connection.
The **wedding** is his biggest money pressure, not AI.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hollis to train him on showroom selling
Cut the wedding guest list from 150 to 110
Swap the honeymoon abroad for a trip to the coast
Keep three months of savings after the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have to compete, so I understand why they'd use it. But I'd also say a company owes something to the people who built it. At church I'd say we look after our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Mr Hollis would hold out longer than most, but not forever. Mr Hollis owns the family firm I work for. If his rivals write catalogues with software overnight, Mr Hollis will have to. And I'm the one writing the catalogues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hollis straight if I could move into the showroom as a salesman, like my dad. I'd push the wedding back maybe six months to save more. And I'd talk to my uncle, who runs a tiling business, about whether he needs someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not hopeless. I can see a way through, it just isn't the way I wanted. I'd feel a bit ashamed asking for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used the AI tools. Would you start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, I'd rather move toward the selling side. The tools would just make me compete with the same tools everyone else has. In the showroom, my dad's way still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Pushing the wedding back. How would Grace feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be upset, and her mum would be more upset. But Grace would understand that we start our marriage without debt. That matters to both of us.

say: I'd say businesses have to **compete**, so I understand it.
I'd say a company **owes something** to the people who built it.
think: Mr Hollis will **hold out** longer than most, but not forever.
He's the one **writing the catalogues** rivals automate.
do: Ask to move into the **showroom as a salesman**, like his dad.
Push the **wedding back** six months to save more.
Ask his **uncle's tiling business** about work.
feel: A bit **ashamed** to ask for help.
S1.quote: Mr Hollis owns the family firm I work for. If his rivals write catalogues with software overnight, Mr Hollis will have to.
fieldNote: He'd skip AI and move toward **showroom selling** instead.
His **free-market** view coexists with loyalty to the firm.
Starting marriage **without debt** shapes his choices.

steps.text: Ask Mr Hollis for a showroom sales job
Move the wedding back six months to save more
Ask his uncle about work at the tiling business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a huge test, and families and churches will have to carry each other. I wouldn't want handouts, but I'd want apprenticeships, fast. At work I'd tell Mr Hollis I'll do whatever's needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my marketing job is finished by 2028. Writing ads is the easiest thing for a machine like that. The showroom might last a few years longer, but selling is talking, and AI can talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my uncle to take me on as a tiling apprentice straight away, because that's hands-on and robots are three years behind. I'd cut everything, and Grace and I would marry quietly at church with just family. We'd move in with her parents for a year to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. I'm not someone who changes quickly. I'd lean on my faith a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said selling is talking and AI can talk. Does that change your showroom plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. A person sitting on a sofa still likes a person beside them, but Mr Hollis would count the cost. Tiling is safer because someone has to kneel on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with Grace's parents. What would that be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her dad's a good man but he likes his routines. It'd be a squeeze in a three-bed with her little brother. But it's what families are for.

say: I'd say **families and churches** will have to carry each other through this.
I'd ask for fast **apprenticeships**, not handouts, and tell Mr Hollis I'll do anything.
think: His marketing job is **finished by 2028**, since ads are easy for AI.
Even showroom **selling is talking**, and AI can talk.
do: Start as a **tiling apprentice** with his uncle straight away.
Marry **quietly at church** with just family.
Move in with **Grace's parents** for a year.
S2.quote: Tiling is safer because someone has to kneel on the floor.
fieldNote: He realises the **showroom** is exposed too, and changes plan.
**Family and church** are his safety net, not the state.
The **robot delay** makes tiling his three-year bridge.

steps.text: Start a tiling apprenticeship with his uncle straight away
Hold a small church wedding with just family
Move in with Grace's parents for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families and businesses to prepare, without the government doing everything. I'd say young men should look at trades. At church I'd help organise something for people who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably wait too long. I'd tell myself Mr Hollis will look after me. Then in year three I'd be scrambling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm being sensible, I'd start learning tiling with my uncle on Saturdays from the first year. We'd still have the wedding, but smaller, and save. By 2029 I'd want to be ready to switch full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, mostly. I know myself, I'm slow to move. Five years feels long until it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You think you'd wait too long. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone at Hollis lose their job. Or Grace telling me straight. She's the one who pushes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at church to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a jobs board, where people with trades offer apprenticeships to younger men and women. Our pastor knows half the builders in town. That's how it should work.

say: I'd say families and businesses should **prepare**, not wait for government.
I'd tell young men to **look at trades**.
think: He'd probably **wait too long**, telling himself Mr Hollis will look after him.
do: Learn **tiling on Saturdays** with his uncle from year one.
S3.quote: Five years feels long until it doesn't.
fieldNote: **Grace** is the one who'd push him to act.
He'd build a **church jobs board** linking local builders with apprentices.

steps.text: Learn tiling with his uncle on Saturdays from the first year
Hold a smaller wedding and save the difference
Help set up a church jobs board for trade apprenticeships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people to stand on their own feet. I'd encourage apprenticeships and family businesses. At work I'd say let's use the time well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd stay at Hollis a good few years. Mr Hollis is near retirement, and maybe his son would keep things as they are. But by 2036, I'd be out of a writing job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Grace next August as planned. I'd move into showroom sales in the next couple of years, and learn tiling on the side from year four. We'd try for children around 30, and I'd want a trade by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. Ten years feels like enough time. Still, it's not the life I pictured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mr Hollis's son might keep things the same. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The owner's son did business at university and talks about efficiency. The owner's son would bring in the AI tools the day he takes over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having children fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a steady trade before we have children. Grace and I have talked about three. That needs a steady wage.

say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to **stand on your own** feet.
think: He'd stay at Hollis **a good few years** while the owner is still there.
By **2036** he'd be out of a writing job.
do: Move into **showroom sales** in two years.
Learn **tiling** on the side from year four.
feel: **Steadier**, but it's not the life he pictured.
S4.quote: The owner's son did business at university and talks about efficiency. The owner's son would bring in the AI tools the day he takes over.
fieldNote: He doubts the **owner's son** will protect jobs.
**Children** are planned around having a trade.
Ten years lets him keep next August's **wedding date** unchanged.

steps.text: Marry Grace next August as planned
Move into showroom sales within two years
Learn tiling with his uncle from year four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I don't change quickly and I'd have a wedding and no job. What would help is quick apprenticeships with a small wage, so men like me could learn a trade without going on benefits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith. People think faith is old-fashioned, but my church would be the first place I'd go if I lost my job.

headlineQuote: People think faith is old-fashioned, but my church would be the first place I'd go if I lost my job.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old marketing assistant** at a family furniture firm, engaged to Grace.
He has **never used AI**, and writes radio ads and catalogues by hand.
His safety net is **family, church** and his uncle's tiling business.
In fast change he'd switch to **tiling**, using the robot delay as a bridge.
He plans **marriage and children** around having a steady trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, facing a wedding with no job and no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Quick apprenticeships** with a small wage, not benefits.
